{{Short description|Highly connected subgraph}}
[[Image:Dense subgraph.png|thumb|An example of a graph {{mvar|G}} with density {{math|1=''d{{sub|G}}'' = 1.375}} and its densest subgraph induced by the vertices {{math|''b'', ''c'', ''d'', ''e''}} and {{mvar|h}} in red with density 1.4 .]]

In [[graph theory]] and [[computer science]], a '''dense subgraph''' is a [[Glossary of graph theory#Subgraphs|subgraph]] with many edges per vertex. This is formalized as follows: let {{math|1=''G'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} be an [[undirected graph]] and let {{math|1=''S'' = (''V{{sub|S}}'', ''E{{sub|S}}'')}} be a subgraph of {{mvar|G}}. Then the ''density'' of {{mvar|S}} is defined to be:
:<math>d(S) = {|E_S|\over|V_S|}</math>

The density of the maximally dense subgraph of a graph is sometimes referred to as its '''subgraph density'''. A subgraph with maximal density can also be seen as a subgraph with maximal average degree in the graph.

Subgraph density is [[Asymptotic complexity|asymptotic]] to the related notion of [[arboricity]] and to [[graph degeneracy]].

== Densest subgraph ==
The '''densest subgraph problem''' is that of finding a subgraph of maximum density. In 1984, [[Andrew V. Goldberg]] developed a [[polynomial time]] algorithm to find the maximum density subgraph using a [[max flow]] technique. This has been improved by Gallo, Grigoriadis and Tarjan in 1989<ref>{{citation |last1=Gallo |first1=Giorgio |title=A fast parametric maximum flow algorithm and applications |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=30–55 |year=1989 |doi=10.1137/0218003 |mr=978165 |last2=Grigoriadis |first2=Michael D. |last3=Tarjan |first3=Robert E.}}</ref> to run in {{math|[[Big O notation|''O'']](''nm'' log(''n''{{sup|2}}/''m''))}} time. A simple LP for finding the optimal solution was given by Charikar in 2000.<ref name=":1">{{citation |last=Charikar |first=Moses |title=Approximation Algorithms for Combinatorial Optimization, Third International Workshop, APPROX 2000, Saarbrücken, Germany, September 5-8, 2000, Proceedings |volume=1913 |pages=84–95 |year=2000 |editor1-last=Jansen |editor1-first=Klaus |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |contribution=Greedy approximation algorithms for finding dense components in a graph |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/3-540-44436-X_10 |isbn=978-3-540-67996-7 |editor2-last=Khuller |editor2-first=Samir}}</ref>

Many of the exact algorithms for solving the densest subgraph problem are impractical on real-world data,<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last1=Boob |first1=Digvijay |last2=Gao |first2=Yu |last3=Peng |first3=Richard |last4=Sawlani |first4=Saurabh |last5=Tsourakakis |first5=Charalampos |last6=Wang |first6=Di |last7=Wang |first7=Junxing |chapter=Flowless: Extracting Densest Subgraphs Without Flow Computations |date=2020-04-20 |title=Proceedings of the Web Conference 2020 |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3366423.3380140 |series=WWW '20 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=573–583 |doi=10.1145/3366423.3380140 |isbn=978-1-4503-7023-3|arxiv=1910.07087 }}</ref> which has led to the study of [[approximation algorithm]]s for the densest subgraph problem. A simple <math display="inline">\frac{1}{2}</math> approximation for finding the densest subgraph was given by Charikar in 2000, based on a peeling procedure which was first proposed by Asahiro, Iwama, Tamaki, and Tokuyama in 1996 as an approximation algorithm for the densest <math>k</math> subgraph problem.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Asahiro |first1=Yuichi |last2=Iwama |first2=Kazuo |last3=Tamaki |first3=Hisao |last4=Tokuyama |first4=Takeshi |date=1996 |editor-last=Karlsson |editor-first=Rolf |editor2-last=Lingas |editor2-first=Andrzej |chapter=Greedily finding a dense subgraph |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-61422-2_127 |title=Algorithm Theory — SWAT'96 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=1097 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=136–148 |doi=10.1007/3-540-61422-2_127 |isbn=978-3-540-68529-6}}</ref> In this algorithm, the vertex with the lowest degree is repeatedly removed, creating an ordering of vertices <math>v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n</math>, where <math>v_i</math> is the <math>i</math>th vertex in the graph to be removed. The subgraph returned by the algorithm is the graph induced by the set <math>S_i = \{v_i, v_{i+1}, \dots, v_n\}</math> with the highest density. By using the dual of the LP for the exact algorithm he provided, Charikar proved that this procedure runs in [[linear time]] and yields a subgraph with at least 50% of the optimal density.<ref name=":1" /> Though 50% is a tight bound, in practice, this greedy peeling procedure yields about 80% of the optimal density on real-world graphs.<ref name=":2" />

In 2020, Boob et al. gave an iterative peeling algorithm that aims to get closer to the optimal subgraph by repeated the peeling procedure multiple times.<ref name=":2" /> Instead of removing the vertices based on their current degree, a load is assigned to each vertex based on data from previous iterations, and vertices are peeled based on their loads. In 2022, Chekuri, Quanrud, and Torres proved that this procedure converges to a <math>(1 - \epsilon)</math> approximation for the densest subgraph problem after <math display="inline">O(\frac{\Delta \log n}{\lambda^* \epsilon^2})</math> iterations of the algorithm, where <math display="inline">\lambda^*</math> is the optimal density and <math>\Delta</math> is the maximum degree in the graph.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Chekuri |first1=Chandra |chapter=Densest Subgraph: Supermodularity, Iterative Peeling, and Flow |date=January 2022 |title=Proceedings of the 2022 Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) |pages=1531–1555 |chapter-url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611977073.64 |access-date=2024-12-12 |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |doi=10.1137/1.9781611977073.64 |last2=Quanrud |first2=Kent |last3=Torres |first3=Manuel R.|isbn=978-1-61197-707-3 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> They also showed that a similar algorithm could be used to find densest [[hypergraph]]s.

==Densest {{mvar|k}} subgraph==
There are many variations on the densest subgraph problem. One of them is the densest {{mvar|k}} subgraph problem, where the objective is to find the maximum density subgraph on exactly {{mvar|k}} vertices. This problem generalizes the [[clique problem]] and is thus [[NP-hard]] in general graphs. There exists a polynomial algorithm approximating the densest {{mvar|k}} subgraph within a ratio of <math>n^{1/4 \,+\, \epsilon}</math> for every <math>\epsilon > 0</math>,<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Bhaskara | first1 = Aditya
 | last2 = Charikar | first2 = Moses | author2-link = Moses Charikar
 | last3 = Chlamtáč | first3 = Eden
 | last4 = Feige | first4 = Uriel | author4-link = Uriel Feige
 | last5 = Vijayaraghavan | first5 = Aravindan
 | contribution = Detecting high log-densities—an {{math|''O''(''n''{{sup|1/4}})}} approximation for densest {{mvar|k}}-subgraph
 | doi = 10.1145/1806689.1806719
 | mr = 2743268
 | pages = 201–210
 | publisher = ACM, New York
 | title = STOC'10—Proceedings of the 2010 ACM International Symposium on Theory of Computing
 | year = 2010| isbn = 978-1-4503-0050-6
 | s2cid = 1391318
 }}.</ref> while it does not admit an <math>n^{1/\!\operatorname{polyloglog} n}</math>-approximation in polynomial time unless the [[exponential time hypothesis]] is false.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Manurangsi | first = Pasin
 | contribution = Almost-polynomial ratio ETH-hardness of approximating densest k-subgraph
 | doi = 10.1145/3055399.3055412
 | pages = 954–961
 | publisher = ACM
 | title = STOC'17—Proceedings of the 49th Annual ACM SIGACT Symposium on Theory of Computing
 | year = 2017| arxiv = 1611.05991
 | isbn = 978-1-4503-4528-6
 | s2cid = 1892186
 }}.</ref> Under a weaker assumption that <math>\mathsf{NP} \nsubseteq \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \mathsf{BPTIME}(2^{n^\epsilon})</math>, no [[Polynomial time approximation scheme|PTAS]] exists for the problem.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Khot | first = Subhash | author-link = Subhash Khot
 | doi = 10.1137/S0097539705447037
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Computing]]
 | mr = 2272270
 | pages = 1025–1071
 | title = Ruling out PTAS for graph min-bisection, dense {{mvar|k}}-subgraph, and bipartite clique
 | volume = 36
 | year = 2006| s2cid = 16514252 }}.</ref>

The problem remains NP-hard in [[bipartite graph]]s and [[chordal graph]]s but is polynomial for [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]] and [[split graph]]s.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Corneil | first1 = D. G. | author1-link = Derek Corneil
 | last2 = Perl | first2 = Y.
 | doi = 10.1016/0166-218X(84)90088-X
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Discrete Applied Mathematics]]
 | mr = 754426
 | pages = 27–39
 | title = Clustering and domination in perfect graphs
 | volume = 9
 | year = 1984| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> It is open whether the problem is NP-hard or polynomial in [[Interval graph|(proper) interval graphs]] and [[planar graph]]s; however, a variation of the problem in which the subgraph is required to be connected is NP-hard in planar graphs.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Keil | first1 = J. Mark
 | last2 = Brecht | first2 = Timothy B.
 | journal = Journal of Combinatorial Mathematics and Combinatorial Computing
 | mr = 1111849
 | pages = 155–159
 | title = The complexity of clustering in planar graphs
 | url = https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~brecht/papers/jcmcc-1991.pdf
 | volume = 9
 | year = 1991}}.</ref>

==Densest at most {{mvar|k}} subgraph==
The objective of the densest at most <math>k</math> problem is to find the maximum density subgraph on at most <math>k</math> vertices. Andersen and Chellapilla showed that if there exists an <math>\alpha</math>-approximation for this problem then that will lead to an <math>\Theta(\alpha^2)</math>-approximation for the densest <math>k</math> subgraph problem.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Andersen |first1=Reid |last2=Chellapilla |first2=Kumar |date=2009 |editor-last=Avrachenkov |editor-first=Konstantin |editor2-last=Donato |editor2-first=Debora |editor3-last=Litvak |editor3-first=Nelly |chapter=Finding Dense Subgraphs with Size Bounds |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-95995-3_3 |title=Algorithms and Models for the Web-Graph |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=25–37 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-95995-3_3 |isbn=978-3-540-95995-3}}</ref> Later, this was improved by [[Samir Khuller|Khuller]] and [[Barna Saha|Saha]] who showed that an <math>\alpha</math>-approximation for densest at most <math>k</math> subgraph implies a <math>4 \alpha</math>-approximation for the densest <math>k</math> subgraph problem.<ref name=":0" />

==Densest at least {{mvar|k}} subgraph==
The densest at least <math> k </math> problem is defined similarly to the densest at most <math>k</math> subgraph problem. The problem is NP-complete,<ref name=":0">{{citation
 | last1 = Khuller | first1 = Samir | author-link = Samir Khuller
 | last2 = Saha | first2 = Barna | author2-link = Barna Saha
 | contribution = On finding dense subgraphs
 | contribution-url = http://www.cs.umd.edu/~samir/grant/ICALP09.pdf
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-02927-1_50
 | location = Berlin
 | mr = 2544878
 | pages = 597–608
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Automata, Languages and Programming: 36th International Colloquium, ICALP 2009, Rhodes, Greece, July 5-12, 2009, Proceedings, Part I
 | volume = 5555
 | year = 2009| isbn = 978-3-642-02926-4 }}</ref> but admits 2-approximation in polynomial time.<ref>{{citation |last=Andersen |first=Reid |title=Finding large and small dense subgraphs |year=2007 |arxiv=cs/0702032 |bibcode=2007cs........2032A}}</ref> Moreover, there is some evidence that this approximation algorithm is essentially the best possible: assuming the [[small set expansion hypothesis]] (a computational complexity assumption closely related to the [[unique games conjecture]]), then it is NP-hard to approximate the problem to within <math>(2 - \epsilon)</math> factor for every constant <math>\epsilon > 0</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Manurangsi | first = Pasin
 | arxiv = 1705.03581
 | doi = 10.3390/a11010010
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Algorithms
 | mr = 3758880
 | page = 10
 | title = Inapproximability of maximum biclique problems, minimum {{mvar|k}}-cut and densest at-least-{{mvar|k}}-subgraph from the small set expansion hypothesis
 | volume = 11
 | year = 2018
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref>

=={{mvar|K}}-clique densest subgraph==
[[Charalampos Tsourakakis]] introduced the <math>k</math>-clique densest subgraph problem. This variation of the densest subgraph problem aims to maximize the average number of induced <math>k</math> cliques <math> d_{k}(S) = {|C_k(S)|\over|V_S|} </math>, where <math>C_k(S)</math> is the set of <math>k</math>-cliques induced by <math>S</math>. Notice that the densest subgraph problem is obtained as a special case for <math>k=2</math>. This generalization provides an empirically successful poly-time approach for extracting large near-cliques from large-scale real-world networks.

==Locally top-{{mvar|k}} densest subgraph==
Qin et al. introduced the problem of top-''k'' locally densest subgraphs discovery in a graph, each of which achieves the highest density in its local region in the graph: it is neither contained in any supergraph with the same or larger density, nor it contains subgraphs with density being loosely connected with the rest of the local densest subgraph. Note that the densest subgraph problem is obtained as a special case for <math>k=1</math>. The set of locally densest subgraphs in
a graph can be computed in polynomial time.
